The following conditions on a functor $F \in \mathrm{Fun}(\mathcal{C}, \mathrm{Sp}_{\geq d}) \subset \mathrm{Fun}(\mathcal{C}, \mathrm{Sp})$ are equivalent: \begin{enumerate} \item $F$ is pseudocoherent. \item For each $n \in \mathbb{Z}$, the functor $\tau_{\leq n} F$ is a compact object of the $\infty$-category $\mathrm{Fun}(\mathcal{C}, \mathrm{Sp}_{\leq n})$. \item There exists a sequence $G_{d-1} = 0 \to G_d \to G_{d+1} \to G_{d+2} \to \dots $ such that $G_i/G_{i-1}$ is a finite direct sum of functors of the form $\Sigma^i \Sigma^\infty_+ \mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}}(C, \cdot)$ for $C \in \mathcal{C}$ and such that $\varinjlim_i G_i \simeq F$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.label: pscohcompact

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 4.3
nodes.statement_short: Cycle of implications; (2)=>(3) builds a cell filtration by killing homotopy one degree at a time.
nodes.statement: Without loss of generality, we can assume $d =0 $ by shifting. For (1) $\Rightarrow$ (2), suppose that $F\in \mathrm{Fun}(\mathcal{C}, \mathrm{Sp})$ (we do not need $F$ connective) is pseudocoherent and let $n\in\mathbb Z$. Then by definition there is a perfect functor $F'$ and a map $F' \to F$ inducing an equivalence $\tau_{\leq n} F' \simeq \tau_{\leq n} F$. Since $\tau_{\leq n}: \mathrm{Fun}(\mathcal{C}, \mathrm{Sp}) \to \mathrm{Fun}(\mathcal{C}, \mathrm{Sp}_{\leq n})$ preserves compact objects (as its right adjoint preserves filtered colimits), it follows that $\tau_{\leq n} F \in \mathrm{Fun}(\mathcal{C}, \mathrm{Sp}_{\leq n})$ is compact. For (2) $\Rightarrow$ (3), suppose that $F \in \mathrm{Fun}(\mathcal{C}, \mathrm{Sp}_{\geq 0})$ and $\tau_{\leq n} F \in \mathrm{Fun}(\mathcal{C}, \mathrm{Sp}_{\leq n})$ is compact for each $n$. Then, by assumption $\tau_{\leq 0} F \in \mathrm{Fun}(\mathcal{C}, \mathrm{Ab}) \subset \mathrm{Fun}(\mathcal{C}, \mathrm{Sp}_{\leq 0})$ is a compact object and thus $\pi_0 F$ is a finitely generated functor. We can thus find a functor $G \in \mathrm{Fun}(\mathcal{C}, \mathrm{Sp}_{\geq 0})$ which is a direct sum of $\Sigma^\infty_+ \mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}}(X, \cdot)$, for finitely many $X\in\mathcal C$, and a map $G \to F$ which is a surjection on $\pi_0$. Let $F_1 $ be the resulting cofiber and observe that $F_1$ has the same property as $F$ (namely $\tau_{\leq n} F_1 \in \mathrm{Fun}(\mathcal{C}, \mathrm{Sp}_{\leq n})$ is compact for each $n$, since compact objects are closed under pushouts) and that $F_1 $ is connected. Continuing in this way, we find a sequence of functors $F \to F_1 \to F_2 \to \dots $ such that $F_n$ is concentrated in degrees $\geq n$ and such that the cofiber of each $F_n \to F_{n+1}$ is a finite direct sum of shifts of representables. We obtain the desired sequence $G_n$ by setting $G_n=\operatorname{Fib}(F\to F_{n+1})$. For (3) $\Rightarrow$ (1), note that each $G_n$ is perfect by induction on $n$, and that $G_{n+1}\rightarrow F$ is an equivalence on $\tau_{\leq n}$.

nodes.name: D-perfect, D-pseudocoherent and D-finitely generated functors
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{D} \subset \mathcal{C}$ be a small full subcategory of a (possibly large, but locally small) category $\mathcal{C}$. Let $F: \mathcal{C} \to \mathrm{Sp}$ be a functor. \begin{enumerate} \item We say that $F$ is \emph{$\mathcal{D}$-perfect} if $F$ belongs to the thick subcategory of $\mathrm{Fun}(\mathcal C,\mathrm{Sp})$ generated by the functors $\Sigma^\infty_+ \mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}}(D, \cdot)$ for $D \in \mathcal{D}$. \item We say that a functor $F: \mathcal{C} \to \mathrm{Sp}$ is called \emph{$\mathcal{D}$-pseudocoherent} if for each $n \in \mathbb{Z}$, there exists a $\mathcal{D}$-perfect functor $F'$ and a map $F' \to F$ such that $\tau_{\leq n} F'(C) \to \tau_{\leq n} F(C)$ is an equivalence for all $C \in \mathcal{C}$. \item A functor $F_0: \mathcal{C} \to \mathrm{Ab}$ is called \emph{$\mathcal{D}$-finitely generated} if there is a surjection as in \eqref{fingenfun} with $X_i \in \mathcal{D}$ for each $i$. \end{enumerate}

nodes.name: Left Kan extension
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{D} \subset \mathcal{C}$ be a full subcategory. Given a functor $G: \mathcal{D} \to \mathrm{Sp}$, we can form the \emph{left Kan extension} $\mathrm{Lan}(G):\mathcal{C} \to \mathrm{Sp}$ (cf. \cite[Sec.~4.3]{HTT}). By definition, for $C \in \mathcal{C}$, $\mathrm{Lan}(G)(C)$ is the colimit $$ \mathrm{Lan}(G)(C) = \varinjlim_{D \to C, D \in \mathcal{D}} G(D) \in \mathrm{Sp}.$$ The construction $F \mapsto \mathrm{Lan}(F)$ is the left adjoint of the forgetful functor $\mathrm{Fun}(\mathcal{C}, \mathrm{Sp}) \to \mathrm{Fun}(\mathcal{D}, \mathrm{Sp})$. A functor $F \in \mathrm{Fun}(\mathcal{C}, \mathrm{Sp})$ is said to be \emph{left Kan extended} from $\mathcal{D}$ if the natural map $\mathrm{Lan}( F|_{\mathcal{D}}) \to F$ is an equivalence in $\mathrm{Fun}(\mathcal{C}, \mathrm{Sp})$. The objects of $\mathrm{Fun}(\mathcal{C}, \mathrm{Sp})$ which are left Kan extended from $\mathcal{D}$ form a subcategory equivalent to $\mathrm{Fun}(\mathcal{D}, \mathrm{Sp})$ (via restriction).

nodes.name: D-pseudocoherence via left Kan extension
conclusions: is $\mathcal{D}$-pseudocoherent if and only if it is left Kan extended from $\mathcal{D}$ and $F|_{\mathcal{D}}: \mathcal{D} \to \mathrm{Sp}$ is pseudocoherent
nodes.statement: A functor $F: \mathcal{C} \to \mathrm{Sp}$ is $\mathcal{D}$-pseudocoherent if and only if it is left Kan extended from $\mathcal{D}$ and $F|_{\mathcal{D}}: \mathcal{D} \to \mathrm{Sp}$ is pseudocoherent.
nodes.label: lkanpscoh

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 4.6
nodes.statement_short: Corepresentables from D are left Kan extended; truncations detect left Kan extension; converse by Kan extending approximations.
nodes.statement: The functor $\Sigma^\infty_+ \mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}}(D, \cdot) \in \mathrm{Fun}(\mathcal{C}, \mathrm{Sp})$ for $D \in \mathcal{D}$ is left Kan extended from $\mathcal{D}$, so a thick subcategory argument shows that any $\mathcal{D}$-perfect functor is left Kan extended from $\mathcal{D}$. To get the same for any $\mathcal{D}$-pseudocoherent functor, note that the truncations $\mathrm{Sp}\rightarrow \mathrm{Sp}_{\leq n}$ are a conservative family of colimit-preserving functors, so a functor to $\mathrm{Sp}$ is left Kan extended if and only if its image in each $\mathrm{Sp}_{\leq n}$ is. Conversely, suppose that $F$ is left Kan extended from $\mathcal{D}$ and $F|_{\mathcal{D}}: \mathcal{D} \to \mathrm{Sp}$ is pseudocoherent. Then $\tau_{\leq n}F\mid_\mathcal{D}\simeq \tau_{\leq n}G\mid_\mathcal{D}$ for some $G:\mathcal{C}\rightarrow\mathrm{Sp}$ in the thick subcategory generated by the $\Sigma^\infty_+ \mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}}(D, \cdot)$, and we deduce $\tau_{\leq n}F\simeq \tau_{\leq n}G$ by left Kan extension.

nodes.name: Cell-filtration characterization of D-pseudocoherence
assumptions: Let $\mathcal{D} \subset \mathcal{C}$ be a small full subcategory.
Let $F: \mathcal{C} \to \mathrm{Sp}_{\geq d}$ be a functor for some $d \in \mathbb{Z}$.
conclusions: the following are equivalent
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{D} \subset \mathcal{C}$ be a small full subcategory. Let $F: \mathcal{C} \to \mathrm{Sp}_{\geq d}$ be a functor for some $d \in \mathbb{Z}$. Then the following are equivalent: \begin{enumerate} \item $F$ is $\mathcal{D}$-pseudocoherent. \item There exists a sequence $G_{d-1} = 0 \to G_d \to G_{d+1} \to G_{d+2} \to \dots $ such that $G_i/G_{i-1}$ is a finite direct sum of functors of the form $\Sigma^i \Sigma^\infty_+ \mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}}(D, \cdot)$ for $D \in \mathcal{D}$ and such that $\varinjlim_i G_i \simeq F$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.label: pscohfilt2

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 4.7
nodes.statement_short: Combine Lemmas 4.6 and 4.3.
nodes.statement: Combine Lemmas~\ref{lkanpscoh} and \ref{pscohcompact}.

nodes.name: Closure properties of D-pseudocoherent functors
nodes.statement_short: D-pseudocoherent functors form a thick subcategory closed under skeletally finite colimits, geometric realizations and smash products, with finitely generated bottom homotopy.
assumptions: Let $\mathcal C$ be a category and $\mathcal{D} \subset \mathcal{C}$ a small full subcategory.
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal C$ be a category and $\mathcal{D} \subset \mathcal{C}$ a small full subcategory. \begin{enumerate} \item The subcategory of $\mathrm{Fun}(\mathcal{C}, \mathrm{Sp})$ spanned by the $\mathcal{D}$-pseudocoherent functors is thick. \item Let $d \in \mathbb{Z}$, let $K$ be a simplicial set, and let $f: K \to \mathrm{Fun}(\mathcal{C}, \mathrm{Sp}_{\geq d})$ be a $K$-indexed diagram of functors $\mathcal{C} \to \mathrm{Sp}_{\geq d}$. Suppose that the $n$-skeleton $\mathrm{sk}_n K$ is a finite simplicial set for every $n\in\mathbb Z$ and that for each vertex $k_0 \in K_0$, the functor $f(k_0) \in \mathrm{Fun}(\mathcal{C}, \mathrm{Sp})$ is $\mathcal{D}$-pseudocoherent. Then the functor $\varinjlim_K f \in \mathrm{Fun}(\mathcal{C}, \mathrm{Sp})$ is $\mathcal{D}$-pseudocoherent. \item Let $d \in \mathbb{Z}$, and let $F_\bullet:\Delta^\sub{op}\to \mathrm{Fun}(\mathcal{C}, \mathrm{Sp}_{\geq d})$ be a simplicial object in the category of functors $\mathcal{C} \to \mathrm{Sp}_{\geq d}$. Suppose that $F_i$ is $\mathcal{D}$-pseudocoherent for every $i \geq 0$. Then the geometric realization $|F_\bullet|: \mathcal{C} \to \mathrm{Sp}$ is $\mathcal{D}$-pseudocoherent. \item Let $d\in \mathbb Z$, and let $F\in \mathrm{Fun}(\mathcal{C}, \mathrm{Sp})$ be a $\mathcal{D}$-pseudocoherent functor such that $\pi_nF=0$ for all $n<d$. Then $\pi_d F: \mathcal{C} \to \mathrm{Ab}$ is a $\mathcal{D}$-finitely generated functor. \item If $\mathcal{C}$ has finite coproducts and $\mathcal{D}$ is closed under them, then the subcategory of $\mathcal{D}$-pseudocoherent functors in $\mathrm{Fun}(\mathcal{C}, \mathrm{Sp})$ is closed under smash products. \end{enumerate}
nodes.label: general:pscoh

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 4.8
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to C = D and use the compactness characterization of Lemma 4.3 for each closure property.
nodes.statement: Thanks to Lemma~\ref{lkanpscoh}, we may assume without loss of generality that $\mathcal{C} = \mathcal{D}$, since the property of being left Kan extended is preserved under all colimits. We may also take $d = 0$. Claim (1) follows from Lemma~\ref{pscohcompact} because compact objects (of any $\infty$-category) are closed under finite colimits and retracts. For (2), it suffices by Lemma~\ref{pscohcompact} to show that $\tau_{\leq n} ( \varinjlim_K f )$ is compact as an object of $\mathrm{Fun}(\mathcal{C}, \mathrm{Sp}_{\leq n})$ for each $n$. But $\tau_{\leq n} f = \tau_{\leq n} ( \varinjlim_{\mathrm{sk}^{n+1} K } f)$ and $\varinjlim_{\mathrm{sk}^{n+1} K } f$ is a finite colimit of pseudocoherent functors, hence pseudocoherent itself by (1); this implies the desired compactness assertion. Claim (3) is handled similarly, because $\tau_{\leq n} ( |F_\bullet|) \simeq \tau_{\leq n} ( \varinjlim_{\Delta_{\leq n+1} }F)$ can be computed as a truncated geometric realization, and this is a finite colimit, cf.~\cite[Lemma~1.2.4.17]{HA}. Claim (4) follows from the filtration Lemma~\ref{pscohcompact}. For (5), it suffices to observe that the smash products of functors of the form $\{\Sigma^\infty_+ \mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}}(X, \cdot)\}_{X \in \mathcal{D}}$ are still of this form under the assumption that $\mathcal{C}$ has finite coproducts and $\mathcal{D} \subset \mathcal{C}$ is closed under them. It then follows by a thick subcategory argument that the subcategory of $\mathcal{D}$-perfect functors is closed under smash products, which implies the analogous assertion for $\mathcal{D}$-pseudocoherent functors.

nodes.name: Goodwillie tower of Sigma^infty Omega^infty
nodes.statement_short: A natural tower P_n under Sigma^infty Omega^infty with layers (X^{tensor n})_{h Sigma_n}, converging for connected X.
conclusions: There is a natural tower
nodes.statement: There is a natural tower $\left\{P_n=P_n ( \Sigma^\infty \Omega^\infty)\right\}_{n \geq 0}$ of functors $\mathrm{Sp} \to \mathrm{Sp}$ receiving a map from $\Sigma^\infty \Omega^\infty$, \[ \Sigma^\infty \Omega^\infty X \to \{ \dots \to P_n (X) \to P_{n-1}(X) \to \dots \to P_1(X) \} \] such that: \begin{enumerate} \item $P_1(X) \simeq X$ and the fiber of $P_n (X) \to P_{n-1} (X) $ is naturally equivalent to $(X^{\otimes n})_{h \Sigma_n}$. \item If $X \in \mathrm{Sp}_{\geq 1}$, the map $\Sigma^\infty \Omega^\infty X \to \varprojlim_n P_n (X)$ is an equivalence and the connectivity of $\Sigma^\infty \Omega^\infty X \to P_n(X)$ tends to $\infty$ with $n$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.label: goodwilliefilt

nodes.name: Pseudocoherence of F versus Sigma^infty Omega^infty F
assumptions: Let $\mathcal{C}$ be a category with finite coproducts and let $\mathcal{D} \subset \mathcal{C}$ be a small subcategory closed under finite coproducts.
$F: \mathcal{C} \to \mathrm{Sp}_{\geq 1}$ a functor.
conclusions: the following are equivalent
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{C}$ be a category with finite coproducts and let $\mathcal{D} \subset \mathcal{C}$ be a small subcategory closed under finite coproducts. Let $F: \mathcal{C} \to \mathrm{Sp}_{\geq 1}$ a functor. Then the following are equivalent: \begin{enumerate} \item $F$ is $\mathcal{D}$-pseudocoherent. \item $\Sigma^\infty \Omega^\infty F$ is $\mathcal{D}$-pseudocoherent. \item $\Sigma^\infty_+ \Omega^\infty F$ is $\mathcal{D}$-pseudocoherent. \end{enumerate}
nodes.label: suspensionpscoh

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 4.10
nodes.statement_short: Goodwillie tower for one direction, the monadic bar resolution for the converse.
nodes.statement: The equivalence of (2) and (3) follows because $\Sigma^\infty, \Sigma^\infty_+$ differ by the constant functor at $S^0$, which is corepresentable since $\mathcal{C}$ has an initial object in $\mathcal{D}$. Suppose $F$ is $\mathcal{D}$-pseudocoherent. Using Proposition~\ref{goodwilliefilt}, we conclude that $\Sigma^\infty \Omega^\infty F$ is the homotopy limit of a tower whose associated graded is given by $F, (F^{\otimes 2})_{h \Sigma_2}, (F^{\otimes 3})_{h \Sigma_3 }, \dots $. Since $F$ takes values in $\mathrm{Sp}_{\geq 1}$, the connectivity of the associated graded terms tends to $\infty$, so this tower stabilizes in any given finite range. As $F$ is $\mathcal{D}$-pseudocoherent, so are all the graded terms in view of Proposition~\ref{general:pscoh}. It follows that $\Sigma^\infty \Omega^\infty F$ is $\mathcal{D}$-pseudocoherent. Conversely, suppose $\Sigma^\infty \Omega^\infty F$ is $\mathcal{D}$-pseudocoherent. First, recall that the adjunction $(\Sigma^\infty, \Omega^\infty)$ between the $\infty$-categories of pointed spaces and connective spectra is monadic since $\Omega^\infty|_{\mathrm{Sp}_{\geq 0}}$ commutes with sifted colimits \cite[Prop.~1.4.3.9]{HA} and in view of the $\infty$-categorical monadicity theorem \cite[Sec.~4.7.3]{HA}; alternatively, this follows explicitly from delooping machinery going back to \cite{Maygeom}. As a result of monadicity, for any $X \in \mathrm{Sp}_{\geq 0}$, one has a natural simplicial spectrum (the bar resolution) $(\Sigma^\infty \Omega^\infty)^{\bullet + 1} X$ whose geometric realization is equivalent to $X$. Therefore, in our case, we can resolve $F$ via the iterates $(\Sigma^\infty \Omega^\infty)^k F$ for $k \geq 1$. By the previous direction and our assumption, each of these is $\mathcal{D}$-pseudocoherent. Thus we have written $F$ as a geometric realization of $\mathcal{D}$-pseudocoherent functors $\mathcal{C} \to \mathrm{Sp}_{\geq 1}$, so $F$ itself is $\mathcal{D}$-pseudocoherent.

nodes.name: Pseudocoherence can be tested after smashing with HZ
assumptions: Let $\mathcal{D} \subset \mathcal{C}$ be a small subcategory.
Let $F: \mathcal{C} \to \mathrm{Sp}$ be a functor.
conclusions: If $F$ is $\mathcal{D}$-pseudocoherent, then $H\mathbb{Z} \otimes F$ is $\mathcal{D}$-pseudocoherent.
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{D} \subset \mathcal{C}$ be a small subcategory. Let $F: \mathcal{C} \to \mathrm{Sp}$ be a functor. If $F$ is $\mathcal{D}$-pseudocoherent, then $H\mathbb{Z} \otimes F$ is $\mathcal{D}$-pseudocoherent. Conversely, if $F: \mathcal{C} \to \mathrm{Sp}$ is uniformly bounded-below and $H \mathbb{Z} \otimes F$ is $\mathcal{D}$-pseudocoherent, so is $F$.
nodes.label: HZpscoh

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 4.11
nodes.statement_short: Approximate HZ and the sphere by finite spectra in any range.
nodes.statement: The first direction follows because we can approximate $H \mathbb{Z}$ in any range by a finite spectrum. The second direction follows because a thick subcategory argument now implies that if $H \mathbb{Z} \otimes F$ is $\mathcal{D}$-pseudocoherent, so is $\tau_{\leq n} S^0 \otimes F$ for each $n$, and we can approximate $F$ in any given range by $\tau_{\leq n} S^0 \otimes F$.

nodes.name: Compact projective henselian nonunital algebras
nodes.statement:
We will use the notion of pseudocoherence in the case 
where $\mathcal{C}  = \mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}}_R$ and $\mathcal{D} = (\mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}}_R)_{\Sigma}$ is the category of compact projective objects 
obtained by idempotent completing the subcategory
$\{R\left\{x_1, \dots, x_n\right\}^+: n \geq 0\}$ of $ \mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}}_R$.

nodes.name: Projectively finitely generated and projectively pseudocoherent functors
nodes.statement: \begin{enumerate} \item A functor $\mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}}_R \to \mathrm{Ab}$ is \emph{projectively finitely generated} if it is $\mathcal{D}$-finitely generated for $\mathcal{D} = (\mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}}_R)_{\Sigma}$. \item A functor $\mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}}_R \to \mathrm{Sp}$ is \emph{projectively pseudocoherent} if it is $\mathcal{D}$-pseudocoherent for $\mathcal{D} = (\mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}}_R)_\Sigma$. \end{enumerate}

nodes.name: I -> Sigma^infty_+ I^n is projectively pseudocoherent
nodes.statement: For each $n$, the functor $I \mapsto \Sigma^\infty_+ I^n$ (where $I^n$ here denotes the cartesian product of $n$ copies of $I$) is projectively pseudocoherent. Indeed, it is the suspension spectrum of the corepresentable associated to $ R\{x_1,\dots,x_n\}^+ \in (\mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}}_R)_\Sigma$.
nodes.label: ex:pseudocoh

nodes.name: Projectively pseudocoherent functors commute with filtered colimits
nodes.statement: A projectively pseudocoherent functor $\mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}}_R \to \mathrm{Sp}$ commutes with filtered colimits. In fact, the corepresentable functors $I \mapsto \Sigma^\infty_+ I^n$ clearly do, and the result for arbitrary projectively pseudocoherent functors follows because the class of functors $\mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}}_R \to \mathrm{Sp}$ which commute with filtered colimits is stable under all colimits. See also Corollary~\ref{kanextcrit} below.
nodes.label: Moved this around and rephrased language slightly

nodes.name: Gabber's vanishing lemma for finitely generated functors
nodes.statement_short: A projectively finitely generated functor on henselian nonunital rings killing bounded-torsion and Q-algebras, right exact and finitary, vanishes.
assumptions: Let $F_0: \mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}} \to \mathrm{Ab}$ be a projectively finitely generated functor.
$F_0(I) = 0$ if $I \in \mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}}$ is annihilated by an integer $N > 0$.
$F_0$ commutes with filtered colimits.
conclusions: Then $F_0 = 0$.
nodes.statement: Let $F_0: \mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}} \to \mathrm{Ab}$ be a projectively finitely generated functor. Suppose that: \begin{enumerate} \item $F_0(I) = 0$ if $I \in \mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}}$ is annihilated by an integer $N > 0$. \item $F_0(I) = 0$ if $I \in \mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}}$ is a nonunital $\mathbb{Q}$-algebra. \item Given a short exact sequence $I' \to I \twoheadrightarrow \overline{I}$ in $\mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}}$, the sequence $F_0(I') \to F_0(I) \to F_0(\overline{I}) \to 0$ of abelian groups is exact. \item $F_0$ commutes with filtered colimits. \end{enumerate} Then $F_0 = 0$.
nodes.label: gabberlem

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 4.15
nodes.statement_short: Find one N with multiplication by N killing all generators, so F_0(NI) -> F_0(I) is zero; conclude by exactness. Uses that rational free henselian algebras are colimits of the maps [N].
nodes.statement: We will prove the following claim: there exists $N\ge1$ such that, for any $I \in \mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}}$, the inclusion map $i_N:NI\to I$ induces the zero map $0=(i_N)_*: F_0(NI) \to F_0(I)$. Once this is done, the statement of the lemma will follow by applying (1) and (3) to the short exact sequence $NI\to I\to I/NI$. As in Corollary~\ref{rationalhens}, let $[N]: \mathbb{Z}\left\{x_1, \dots, x_n\right\}^+ \to \mathbb{Z}\left\{x_1, \dots, x_n\right\}^+$ be the operator that multiplies each $x_i$ by $N$, so that the colimit of the $[N]$, indexed over $N\ge1$ ordered by divisibility, is $\mathbb{Q}\left\{x_1, \dots, x_n\right\}^+$. By assumption $F_0$ commutes with filtered colimits and annihilates any nonunital henselian $\mathbb{Q}$-algebra; so, given any element $u \in F_0(\mathbb{Z}\left\{x_1, \dots, x_n\right\}^+)$, it follows that there exists $N > 0$ such that $[N]_*(u) = 0$. Now we use that $F_0$ is projectively finitely generated. This means that there exists a surjection \[ \bigoplus_{i=1}^t \mathbb{Z}[\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}}}(\mathbb{Z}\left\{x_1, \dots, x_{n_i}\right\}^+, \cdot)] \to F_0\] of functors for some $n_1,\dots,n_t\ge1$. For each $i=1,\dots,t$, let $g_i\in F_0(\mathbb{Z}\left\{x_1, \dots, x_{n_i}\right\}^+)$ be the image of $\mathrm{id}\in \mathrm{Hom}_{\mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}}}(\mathbb{Z}\left\{x_1, \dots, x_{n_i}\right\}^+, \mathbb{Z}\left\{x_1, \dots, x_{n_i}\right\}^+)$. Then the above surjection concretely means the following: given any $I\in \mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}}$ and any element $y\in F_0(I)$, then $y$ is a finite sum of elements of $F_0(I)$ obtained by pushing forward the $g_i$ along various maps $\phi:\mathbb{Z}\left\{x_1, \dots, x_{n_i}\right\}^+ \to I$. By the second paragraph, there exists an integer $N > 0$ such that $[N]_*(g_i)=0$ for all the generators $g_i$. From this we can easily complete the proof of the claim, as follows. Given any $I \in \mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}}$, every map $\phi: \mathbb{Z}\{ x_1, \dots, x_{n_i}\}^+ \to N I $ has the property that the composite $i_N \circ \phi: \mathbb{Z}\left\{x_1, \dots, x_{n_i}\right\}^+ \to I$ factors through $[N]$, i.e., one has a commutative diagram in $\mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}}$ \[ \xymatrix{ \mathbb{Z}\left\{x_1, \dots, x_n\right\}^+ \ar[r]_-{\phi}\ar[d]^{[N]} & NI \ar[d]^{i_N} \\ \mathbb{Z}\left\{x_1, \dots, x_n\right\}^+ \ar[r] & I }.\] By choice of $N$ it follows that the composite \[ \mathbb{Z}[\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}}}( \mathbb{Z}\left\{x_1, \dots, x_{n_i}\right\}^+, NI)] \to F_0(NI) \to F_0(I) \] is zero. But we have shown that every element of $F_0(NI)$ is a finite sum of elements of the form $\phi_*(g_i)$ for various maps $\phi$. Since $g_i \in F_0( \mathbb{Z}\left\{x_1, \dots, x_{n_i}\right\}^+)$ is annihilated by $[N]$, it follows that $(i_N)_*: F_0(NI) \to F_0(I)$ is zero, as claimed.

nodes.name: Axiomatic rigidity argument
nodes.statement_short: A projectively pseudocoherent functor vanishing on free henselian algebras over prime fields, exact, and nil-invariant, vanishes.
assumptions: Let $F: \mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}} \to \mathrm{Sp}$ be a projectively pseudocoherent functor.
If $I \in \mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}}$ is nilpotent, then $F(I) = 0$.
conclusions: Then $F = 0$.
nodes.statement: Let $F: \mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}} \to \mathrm{Sp}$ be a projectively pseudocoherent functor. Suppose that: \begin{enumerate} \item For each prime field $R$ and each $n$, we have $F( R\left\{x_1, \dots, x_n\right\}^+) = 0$. \item Given a short exact sequence $I' \to I \twoheadrightarrow \overline{I}$ in $\mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}}$, the sequence $F(I') \to F(I) \to F(\overline{I})$ is a fiber sequence of spectra. \item If $I \in \mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}}$ is nilpotent, then $F(I) = 0$. \end{enumerate} Then $F = 0$.
nodes.label: pseudoargument

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 4.16
nodes.statement_short: F vanishes over prime fields by Kan extension, then on bounded torsion; the lowest homotopy functor vanishes by Lemma 4.15.
nodes.statement: Let $R$ be a prime field and restrict $F$ to $\mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}}_R$ to obtain a functor $F_R: \mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}}_R \to \mathrm{Sp}$. We observe first that $F_R$ is projectively pseudocoherent (since the building blocks $I \mapsto \Sigma^\infty_+ I^n$ for projectively pseudocoherent functors $\mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}}_R \to \mathrm{Sp}$ are independent of the base ring $R$). In particular, $F_R$ is left Kan extended from the subcategory $(\mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}}_R)_{\Sigma}$. By assumption, $F_R$ annihilates $(\mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}}_R)_\Sigma$, so that $F_R = 0$ on $\mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}}_R$. It follows that $F$ annihilates any nonunital henselian algebra over a field. Moreover, if $I \in \mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}}$ is such that there exists $N \in \mathbb{Z}_{>0}$ with $NI = 0$, it follows that $F(I) = 0$: in fact, since $F$ preserves finite products we reduce to the case where $N = p^r$ for some $r$, and then use the short exact sequence $pI \to I \to I/p I$ where $pI$ is nilpotent. The resulting fiber sequence then shows that $F(I) \simeq F(I/pI) = 0$. Suppose $F$ is not the zero functor. Let $d$ be minimal such that $\pi_d F \neq 0$. Then $\pi_d F$ is a projectively finitely generated functor $\mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}} \to \mathrm{Ab}$ which commutes with filtered colimits; furthermore, $\pi_d F$ annihilates any $I \in \mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}}$ which is either of bounded torsion or a $\mathbb{Q}$-vector space. Using Lemma~\ref{gabberlem} below, we find that $\pi_d F = 0$, a contradiction.

nodes.name: Left Kan extension via simplicial resolutions
nodes.statement_short: A functor left Kan extended from compact projectives is computed by simplicial resolutions by free henselian nonunital algebras.
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{E}$ be an $\infty$-category that has sifted colimits, fix a base ring $R$ and a functor \[ F: \mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}}_R \to \mathcal{E}, \] and consider the following condition on $F$: \begin{itemize} \item[(Kan)] $F$ is left Kan extended from the subcatgory $(\mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}}_R)_\Sigma \subset \mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}}_R$. \end{itemize} Suppose $F$ satisfies (Kan). Then one can compute $F$ from its values on $(\mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}}_R)_\Sigma$ as follows. First, $F$ commutes with filtered colimits, and hence its value is determined on all free objects in $\mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}}_R$. Next, if $I$ is an arbitrary nonunital henselian $R$-algebra, then there exists an augmented simplicial object $I_\bullet:\Delta^\sub{op}_+ \to \mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}}_R$ such that $I_{-1} = I$, each $I_i$ is a free algebra in $\mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}}_R$, and $|I_\bullet| \simeq I_{-1} = I$, i.e., $I_\bullet$ is a simplicial resolution of $I$ by free objects; then the value of $F$ on $I$ is given by $F(I) = |F(I_\bullet)|$. The construction of such simplicial resolutions (and the independence of choices) is a general homotopical technique going back to Quillen \cite{QuillenHA}, originally developed to build the cotangent complex via simplicial commutative rings. Using the results of \cite{QuillenHA} (which work in particular for any category satisfying (Law) from Remark \ref{remark_Lawvere}, by \cite[Rmk.~1, pg.~II.4.2]{QuillenHA}), we can make the category $\mathrm{Fun}( \Delta^\sub{op}, \mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu}}_R)$ of simplicial nonunital henselian $R$-algebras into a model category where the weak equivalences and fibrations are those of underlying simplicial sets. The resolution $I_\bullet$ of $I$ is then obtained as a cofibrant replacement in this model category of the constant simplicial object $I$. This can also be phrased using the language of nonabelian derived $\infty$-categories \cite[Sec.~5.5.8]{HTT}. We record these observations for the future in the following corollary which does not mention simplicial non-unital henselian rings. \begin{corollary} Let $\mathcal{E}$ be an $\infty$-category with sifted colimits, and let $F: \mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}}_R \to \mathcal{E}$ be a functor. Then the following are equivalent: \begin{enumerate} \item $F$ is left Kan extended from $(\mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}}_R)_{\Sigma} \subset \mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}}_R$. \item Whenever $I_\bullet$ is a simplicial object in $\mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}}_R$ whose geometric realization is equivalent to $I_{-1} \in \mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}}_R$ (in particular, the homotopy type of the underlying simplicial set of $I_\bullet$ is discrete), then the map $|F(I_\bullet)| \to F(I_{-1})$ is an equivalence.\footnote{Since the category of nonunital henselian rings is the category of algebras over a monad on the category of sets, there is always a canonical resolution of any object by free objects; it would suffice to consider these resolutions.} Furthermore, $F$ commutes with filtered colimits. \end{enumerate} \end{corollary}
nodes.label: kanextsifted

nodes.name: Criterion for left Kan extension from compact projectives
assumptions: Let $\mathcal{E}$ be an $\infty$-category with sifted colimits, and let $F: \mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}}_R \to \mathcal{E}$ be a functor.
conclusions: the following are equivalent
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{E}$ be an $\infty$-category with sifted colimits, and let $F: \mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}}_R \to \mathcal{E}$ be a functor. Then the following are equivalent: \begin{enumerate} \item $F$ is left Kan extended from $(\mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}}_R)_{\Sigma} \subset \mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}}_R$. \item Whenever $I_\bullet$ is a simplicial object in $\mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}}_R$ whose geometric realization is equivalent to $I_{-1} \in \mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}}_R$ (in particular, the homotopy type of the underlying simplicial set of $I_\bullet$ is discrete), then the map $|F(I_\bullet)| \to F(I_{-1})$ is an equivalence.\footnote{Since the category of nonunital henselian rings is the category of algebras over a monad on the category of sets, there is always a canonical resolution of any object by free objects; it would suffice to consider these resolutions.} Furthermore, $F$ commutes with filtered colimits. \end{enumerate}
nodes.label: kanextcrit

nodes.name: Singular chains C_*(X; Z)
nodes.statement:
Given a space $X$, we write $C_*(X; \mathbb{Z}) = H\mathbb{Z}\otimes \Sigma^\infty_+ X$ for the singular chains on $X$
with $\mathbb{Z}$-coefficients, viewed as a (generalized) Eilenberg--MacLane spectrum.

nodes.name: Projective pseudocoherence of group homology of GL
nodes.statement_short: I -> C_*(BGL_infty(Z semidirect I); Z) is projectively pseudocoherent.
conclusions: is projectively pseudocoherent
nodes.statement: The functor $ \mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}} \to \mathrm{Sp}$ given by $I \mapsto C_*( BGL_\infty(\mathbb{Z} \ltimes I); \mathbb{Z})$ is projectively pseudocoherent.
nodes.label: glpscoh

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 4.19
nodes.statement_short: Homological stability reduces to GL_n; the bar construction and Borel--Serre finiteness give projective pseudocoherence.
nodes.statement: First, by the homological stability results of Maazen and van der Kallen \cite{vdK}, we can approximate $C_*(BGL_\infty(\mathbb{Z} \ltimes I); \mathbb{Z})$ by $C_*(BGL_n(\mathbb{Z} \ltimes I); \mathbb{Z})$ in any given finite range. It is crucial for us that this stability range is independent of the choice of $I$: namely, the stability range depends on the Krull dimension of the maximal spectrum of $\mathbb{Z} \ltimes I$, but since $I$ is contained in the Jacobson radical this is the maximal spectrum of $\mathbb{Z}$. Thus, it suffices to show that for any $n$, the functor $I \mapsto C_*(BGL_n(\mathbb{Z} \ltimes I); \mathbb{Z})$ is projectively pseudocoherent. We use the short exact sequence of groups \[ 1 \to GL_n(1 + I) \to GL_n( \mathbb{Z} \ltimes I) \to GL_n(\mathbb{Z}) \to 1, \] where $GL_n(1 + I)$ is, by definition, the kernel of the second map in the above sequence. It follows that there is a $GL_n(\mathbb{Z})$-action on $C_*(BGL_n(1 + I); \mathbb{Z})$ and we have \begin{equation} C_*(BGL_n(\mathbb{Z} \ltimes I); \mathbb{Z}) \simeq C_*(BGL_n(1 + I); \mathbb{Z})_{h GL_n(\mathbb{Z})}. \end{equation} We next argue that the functor $I \mapsto C_*(BGL_n(1 + I); \mathbb{Z})$ is projectively pseudocoherent. Note that as a set, $GL_n(1 + I)$ is naturally isomorphic to the cartesian product $I^{n^2}$ since $I$ is contained in the radical of $\mathbb{Z} \ltimes I$. Now we observe that using the classical bar construction and the isomorphism (of sets) $GL_n(1 + I) \simeq I^{n^2}$, that $C_*(BGL_n(1 + I); \mathbb{Z})$ is a geometric realization of functors of the form $I \mapsto \mathbb{Z}[I^{n^2i}]$ for $i \geq 0$. Since the functor $I \mapsto \mathbb{Z}[I^{n^2i}] \simeq H \mathbb{Z} \otimes \Sigma^\infty_+ \mathrm{Hom}_{\mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}}}(\mathbb{Z}\left\{x_1, \dots, x_{n^2i}\right\}^+, I)$ is clearly projectively pseudocoherent, it follows that $I \mapsto C_*(BGL_n(1 +I); \mathbb{Z})$ is projectively pseudocoherent as desired. Finally, the group $GL_n(\mathbb{Z})$ admits a finite index normal subgroup $N \leq GL_n(\mathbb{Z})$ such that $BN$ has the homotopy type of a finite CW complex, by the existence of the Borel-Serre compactification (see \cite{Serresurvey} for a survey). Since $(-)_{hGL_n(\mathbb{Z})} \simeq ((-)_{hN})_{h(G/N)}$, we conclude by two applications of Proposition \ref{general:pscoh} that taking $GL_n(\mathbb{Z})$-homotopy orbits preserves projective pseudocoherence. Therefore, we conclude in view of the previous paragraph and \eqref{glnZorbit}.

nodes.name: Homotopy orbit formula for C_*(BGL_n)
nodes.statement: C_*(BGL_n(\mathbb{Z} \ltimes I); \mathbb{Z}) \simeq C_*(BGL_n(1 + I); \mathbb{Z})_{h GL_n(\mathbb{Z})}.
nodes.label: glnZorbit

nodes.name: K_0 is invariant for henselian pairs
assumptions: Let $(R, I)$ be a henselian pair.
conclusions: $K_0(R) \simeq K_0(R/I)$
nodes.statement: Let $(R, I)$ be a henselian pair. Then $K_0(R) \simeq K_0(R/I)$.
nodes.label: K0invhenspair

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 4.20
nodes.statement_short: Lift isomorphisms by Nakayama and lift projectives by idempotent lifting.
nodes.statement: In fact, we claim that isomorphism classes of finitely generated projective $R$ modules and isomorphism classes of finitely generated projective $R/I$-modules agree. For one direction, if $M, N$ are finitely generated projective $R$-modules, then any isomorphism $M/IM \simeq N/IM$ can be lifted to a map $M \to N$, which is necessarily an isomorphism by Nakayama's lemma applied to the kernel; we use here that $I$ is contained in the Jacobson radical of $R$. For the other direction, by lifting idempotents any projective $R/I$-module lifts to $R$, cf. \cite[Tag 0D49]{stacks-project}.

nodes.name: Projective pseudocoherence of K-theory
conclusions: is projectively pseudocoherent
nodes.statement: The functor $\mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}} \to \mathrm{Sp}$ given by $I \mapsto K( \mathbb{Z} \ltimes I)$ is projectively pseudocoherent.
nodes.label: Kpscoh

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 4.21
nodes.statement_short: K_0 is constant; reduce via the plus construction to Proposition 4.19.
nodes.statement: Since $I$ is henselian, we have $K_0( \mathbb{Z} \ltimes I) = \mathbb{Z}$ by Lemma \ref{K0invhenspair}; since the constant functor $\mathbb{Z}$ is projectively pseudocoherent, it remains to see that the functor $I \mapsto \tau_{\geq 1} K(\mathbb{Z} \ltimes I)$ is projectively pseudocoherent. By Propositions \ref{suspensionpscoh} and \ref{HZpscoh} and the plus-construction description of $K$-theory (cf.~\cite[IV.1]{KBook} for an account), it suffices to check that the functor \[I \mapsto H \mathbb{Z} \otimes \Sigma^\infty_+ \Omega^\infty \tau_{\geq 1} K(\mathbb{Z} \ltimes I) \simeq C_*(BGL_\infty(\mathbb{Z} \ltimes I); \mathbb{Z})\] is projectively pseudocoherent, which follows from Proposition~\ref{glpscoh} above.

nodes.name: K-theory commutes with simplicial resolutions of nonunital local rings
nodes.statement: In particular, Proposition \ref{Kpscoh} shows that the functor $\mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}} \to \mathrm{Sp}$, $I \mapsto K( \mathbb{Z} \ltimes I)$ commutes with simplicial resolutions in view of Construction~\ref{kanextsifted}. The same argument shows that this also holds in the larger category of nonunital local rings, even without the henselian condition. This observation, in various forms, plays an important role in the study of the local structure of $K$-theory. Compare, for instance \cite[Lemma I.2.2]{Goodrel} for the nilpotent case and \cite[Ch.~III, Prop.~1.4.2]{dgm} for a more general assertion for radical pairs.

nodes.name: Eilenberg--MacLane functor is projectively pseudocoherent
conclusions: is projectively pseudocoherent
nodes.statement: The Eilenberg--MacLane functor $\mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}} \to \mathrm{Sp}$ given by $I \mapsto HI$ is projectively pseudocoherent.
nodes.label: EMpscoh

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 4.23
nodes.statement_short: Direct consequence of Lemma 4.24 for abelian groups.
nodes.statement:
Lemma~\ref{EMpscoh} is a direct consequence of the following result, in the
context of abelian groups.

nodes.name: A -> HA is Latt-pseudocoherent
assumptions: Let $\mathrm{Ab}$ be the category of abelian groups.
conclusions: The functor $\mathrm{Ab} \to \mathrm{Sp}$ given by $A \mapsto HA$ is $\mathrm{Latt}$-pseudocoherent
nodes.statement: Let $\mathrm{Ab}$ be the category of abelian groups. The functor $\mathrm{Ab} \to \mathrm{Sp}$ given by $A \mapsto HA$ is $\mathrm{Latt}$-pseudocoherent for $\mathrm{Latt} \subset \mathrm{Ab}$ the subcategory of finitely generated free abelian groups.
nodes.label: Abpscoh

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 4.24
nodes.statement_short: Write HA as a colimit of suspension spectra of Eilenberg--MacLane spaces and use iterated bar constructions.
nodes.statement: We can write functorially $HA = \varinjlim_n \Sigma^{-n}\Sigma^\infty K(A, n)$ for $K(A, n)$ the $n$th Eilenberg--MacLane space for $A$. This colimit stabilizes in any ranges of degrees by the Freudenthal suspension theorem, so it suffices to show that the functor $A \mapsto \Sigma^\infty K(A, n)$ is projectively pseudocoherent. But this follows from the iterated bar construction which gives a functorial model for $K(A, n)$ as the colimit of an $n$-fold simplicial space each of whose terms is a product of copies of $A$.

nodes.name: Deligne's functorial free resolution
nodes.statement_short: Every abelian group has a functorial resolution by finite sums of free abelian groups Z[A^n].
nodes.statement:
In the setting of $H\mathbb{Z}$-modules rather than
spectra, 
Lemma~\ref{Abpscoh}
is an unpublished result of Deligne, which states that any abelian group $A$ has a
functorial resolution by free abelian groups all of whose terms are finite direct sums of the
form $\mathbb{Z}[A^n]$.

nodes.name: Projective pseudocoherence of THH
conclusions: is projectively pseudocoherent
nodes.statement: The functor $\mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}} \to \mathrm{Sp}$ given by $I \mapsto \mathrm{THH}( \mathbb{Z} \ltimes I)$ is projectively pseudocoherent.
nodes.label: THHps

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 4.25
nodes.statement_short: Cyclic bar construction and Lemma 4.23.
nodes.statement: Using the cyclic bar construction for $\mathrm{THH}$, this follows because all the terms $(H(\mathbb{Z} \ltimes I))^{\otimes k}$ (of which $\mathrm{THH}$ is a geometric realization) are projectively pseudocoherent in view of Lemma~\ref{EMpscoh} and Proposition~\ref{general:pscoh}.

nodes.name: Projective pseudocoherence of TC/p
conclusions: is projectively pseudocoherent
nodes.statement: The functor $\mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}} \to \mathrm{Sp}$ given by $I \mapsto \mathrm{TC}( \mathbb{Z} \ltimes I)/p$ is projectively pseudocoherent.
nodes.label: TCpscoh

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 4.26
nodes.statement_short: Combine Lemma 4.25 with Proposition 2.19.
nodes.statement: This now follows from Lemma~\ref{THHps} and Proposition~\ref{strong:finiteness}. Indeed, for any of the functors $F$ in the statement of the latter, we have that $I \mapsto F( \mathrm{THH}(\mathbb{Z} \ltimes I))$ is projectively pseudocoherent (note that taking $S^1$-homotopy orbits preserves pseudocoherence thanks to Lemma~\ref{general:pscoh}, as the skeleta of $BS^1$ are finite complexes), and then we can approximate $\mathrm{TC}/p$ in any range.

nodes.name: nu^n and its cokernel variant
nodes.statement_short: nu^n(R) = ker(1 - C^{-1}) on n-forms (the logarithmic forms), and nu~^n(R) its cokernel.
nodes.statement: For an $\mathbb{F}_p$-algebra $R$, we let $\nu^n(R) = \ker( 1 - C^{-1}: \Omega^n_R \to \Omega^n_R / d \Omega^{n-1}_R)$. We will also write this as $\Omega^n_{R, \mathrm{log}}$. We also let $\widetilde{\nu^n}(R)$ be the cokernel of $1 - C^{-1}$.

nodes.name: nu^n is an etale sheaf
nodes.statement: The construction $\nu^n$ thus defines a sheaf for the \'etale topology.

nodes.name: Proof that nu^n is an etale sheaf
nodes.statement_short: Kernel of a map between quasi-coherent sheaves (Lemma 4.28).
nodes.statement:
To see this, we observe that it is a kernel of a map between two objects, both
of which are quasi-coherent over the Frobenius twist by the next lemma.

nodes.name: nu~^n vanishes etale locally
nodes.statement:
By contrast,
$\widetilde{\nu^n}$ vanishes locally in the \'etale topology since $1 -
C^{-1}$ is surjective locally in the \'etale topology.

nodes.name: Etale base change for forms modulo exact forms
assumptions: Let $R \to S$ be an \'etale map of $\mathbb{F}_p$-algebras.
conclusions: The map $\Omega^n_R \otimes_R S \to \Omega^n_S$ is an isomorphism.
nodes.statement: Let $R \to S$ be an \'etale map of $\mathbb{F}_p$-algebras. Let $R^{(1)} \rightarrow R, S^{(1)} \rightarrow S$ be the Frobenius twists of $R$ and $S$.\footnote{Thus $R^{(1)}$ consists of formal expressions of the form ``$a^p$", and the map to $R$ is ``$a^p$" $\mapsto a^p$. More straightforwardly, we can set $R^{(1)}=R$ and take the map $R^{(1)}=R\rightarrow R$ to be the Frobenius.} Then: \begin{enumerate} \item The map $\Omega^n_R \otimes_R S \to \Omega^n_S$ is an isomorphism. \item The de Rham differentials $d: \Omega^{n-1}_R \to \Omega^n_R, \Omega^{n-1}_S \to \Omega^n_S$ are respectively $R^{(1)}, S^{(1)}$-linear so that the quotients $\Omega^n_R/d \Omega_R^{n-1} , \Omega^n_S/d \Omega_S^{n-1} $ inherit the structure of $R^{(1)}, S^{(1)}$-modules respectively. The map $\Omega^n_R/d \Omega_R^{n-1} \otimes_{R^{(1)}} S^{(1)} \to \Omega^n_S/d\Omega^{n-1}_S$ is an isomorphism. \end{enumerate}
nodes.label: qcohomega

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 4.28
nodes.statement_short: Etale maps make the Frobenius square cocartesian.
nodes.statement: Part (1) is standard. Since $R \to S$ is \'etale, the natural square linking $R^{(1)}, R, S^{(1)}$ and $S$ is cocartesian (cf.~\cite[Tag 0EBS]{stacks-project}), which now implies (2).

nodes.name: Geisser--Levine and Geisser--Hesselholt calculations
nodes.statement_short: For ind-smooth F_p-algebras, K/p is nu^n locally, TC/p is an extension of nu^n by nu~^{n+1}, and K^inv/p is nu~^{n+2} locally.
assumptions: Let $R$ be an ind-smooth $\mathbb{F}_p$-algebra.
nodes.label: GHGL

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 4.29
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to finite type; quote Geisser--Levine, and Geisser--Hesselholt's etale descent with quasi-coherence of forms.
nodes.statement:
First we note that it suffices to prove this theorem in the case where $R$ is essentially of finite type over $\mathbb{F}_p$, by extending using filtered colimits. Then the first assertion follows from \cite[Thm.~8.3]{GL}, which shows that on smooth varieties over $\mathbb{F}_p$, the Zariski sheafification of the presheaf $\pi_n(K(\cdot)/p)$ is given by $
u^n$. The exact sequence describing $\pi_n( \mathrm{TC}(R)/p)$ actually follows from \eqref{thisdiag}, though we will give a slightly different proof of the stronger second claim. Namely, we use the results of Geisser--Hesselholt \cite[Thm.~4.2.6]{GH} that on smooth quasi-compact quasi-separated schemes over $\mathbb{F}_p$, the homotopy group sheaves in the \emph{'etale} topology of $\mathrm{TC}/p$ identify with those of $K/p$ via the cyclotomic trace, and hence identify with the $
u^n$; and moreover one has an 'etale descent spectral sequence starting from the 'etale cohomology of $
u^n$ and converging to $\pi_*( \mathrm{TC}/p)$. In the 'etale topology, there is a short exact sequence of sheaves $0 	o 
u^n 	o \Omega^n \xrightarrow{1 - C^{-1}} \Omega^n/d \Omega^{n-1} 	o 0$, and the second and third terms are quasi-coherent (either over the structure sheaf or its Frobenius twist by Lemma~ef{qcohomega}), so have no higher cohomology on affines. It follows that $H^0( (\mathrm{Spec} R)_{et}, 
u^n) = 
u^n(R), H^1( (\mathrm{Spec} R)_{et}, 
u^n) = \widetilde{
u}^n(R)$, and the 'etale descent spectral sequence thus implies the second claim. The third claim follows from the first two.

nodes.name: Solving x - s x^n = 1 in henselian pairs
assumptions: Let $(R, I)$ be a henselian pair.
Let $s \in I$ and let $n \geq 1$.
conclusions: the equation $x - s x^n = 1$ can be solved in $R$
nodes.statement: Let $(R, I)$ be a henselian pair. Let $s \in I$ and let $n \geq 1$. Then the equation $x - s x^n = 1$ can be solved in $R$.
nodes.label: solveeq:hens

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 4.30
nodes.statement_short: x = 1 is a simple root modulo I and lifts.
nodes.statement: The equation has a simple root in $R/I$ (namely, $x = 1$), which therefore admits a lift to $R$ by definition of henselian.

nodes.name: Rigidity of nu and nu~ for henselian pairs of F_p-algebras
assumptions: Let $(R, I)$ be a henselian pair of $\mathbb{F}_p$-algebras.
conclusions: the map $\nu^n(R) \to \nu^n(R/I)$ is surjective
the map $\widetilde{\nu}^{n}(R) \to \widetilde{\nu}^n(R/I)$ is an isomorphism
nodes.label: toyFprigidityTC

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 4.31
nodes.statement_short: Show V_0 -> V_1 surjective by solving u - u^p c = 1 with Lemma 4.30; conclude by the snake lemma.

nodes.name: Rigidity for ind-smooth henselian local F_p-algebras
assumptions: Let $(R, \mathfrak{m})$ be an ind-smooth henselian local $\mathbb{F}_p$-algebra with residue field $k$.
conclusions: the map $K^{\mathrm{inv}}(R) \to K^{\mathrm{inv}}(k)$ becomes an equivalence modulo $p$
nodes.statement: Let $(R, \mathfrak{m})$ be an ind-smooth henselian local $\mathbb{F}_p$-algebra with residue field $k$. Then the map $K^{\mathrm{inv}}(R) \to K^{\mathrm{inv}}(k)$ becomes an equivalence modulo $p$.
nodes.label: rigidity:henspaircharp

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 4.32
nodes.statement_short: Reduce via Theorem 4.29 to nu~ and apply Proposition 4.31.
nodes.statement: By Theorem~\ref{GHGL}, it suffices to show that the map \( \widetilde{\nu}^n(R) \to \widetilde{\nu}^n(k) \) is an isomorphism. This follows from Proposition~\ref{toyFprigidityTC}.

nodes.name: Nonconnective K^inv
nodes.statement:
For this, we need to invoke the
non-connective variant $\mathbb{K}^{\operatorname{inv}}$ of
$K^{\operatorname{inv}}$, defined as the fiber of the cyclotomic trace
$\mathbb{K}\rightarrow \mathrm{TC}$ from non-connective $K$-theory.

nodes.name: Excision for K^inv (Cortinas; Geisser--Hesselholt; Dundas--Kittang; Land--Tamme)
nodes.statement_short: Relative nonconnective K^inv satisfies excision for Milnor squares.
assumptions: Suppose $R$ is a unital associative ring, $I\subset R$ a two-sided ideal, and $f:R\rightarrow S$ a homomorphism such that $f$ restricts to an isomorphism from $I$ to a two-sided ideal $J$ of $S$
conclusions: is an equivalence
nodes.statement: Suppose $R$ is a unital associative ring, $I\subset R$ a two-sided ideal, and $f:R\rightarrow S$ a homomorphism such that $f$ restricts to an isomorphism from $I$ to a two-sided ideal $J$ of $S$ (so one has a Milnor square, cf.~ Definition~\ref{milnorsquare}). Then the induced map $$\mathbb{K}^{\operatorname{inv}}(R,I)\rightarrow \mathbb{K}^{\operatorname{inv}}(S,J)$$ is an equivalence.
nodes.label: DKGHC

nodes.name: K^inv of a nonunital ring
nodes.statement:
To make this precise, one can define
$\mathbb{K}^{\operatorname{inv}}(I) =
\mathbb{K}^{\operatorname{inv}}(\mathbb{Z}\ltimes I,I)$ for any non-unital
ring $I$.

nodes.name: Nonconnective K^inv is exact on nonunital rings
nodes.statement:
Clearly the new $\mathbb{K}^{\operatorname{inv}}$
restricts to the old one on unital rings; moreover, Theorem  \ref{DKGHC} implies 
that $\mathbb{K}^{\operatorname{inv}}$ sends short exact sequences
$I'\rightarrow I\twoheadrightarrow I''$ of non-unital rings to fiber sequences
of spectra.

nodes.name: K^inv(I) agrees with relative K^inv for any embedding
nodes.statement:
In particular, $\mathbb{K}^{\operatorname{inv}}(I) \simeq
\mathbb{K}^{\operatorname{inv}}(R,I)$ whenever $I$ embeds as a two-sided ideal
in $R$, in view of Theorem~\ref{DKGHC} applied to the map $(\mathbb{Z} \oplus I, I) \to (R, I)$ of pairs of
rings with an ideal.

nodes.name: Connective versus nonconnective relative K-theory for henselian Milnor squares
assumptions: Suppose $(R,I)$ is a henselian pair, and $f:R\rightarrow S$ is a ring homomorphism such that $f$ restricts to an isomorphism from $I$ to an ideal $J$ of $S$.
conclusions: is cartesian
nodes.statement: Suppose $(R,I)$ is a henselian pair, and $f:R\rightarrow S$ is a ring homomorphism such that $f$ restricts to an isomorphism from $I$ to an ideal $J$ of $S$. Then the square of spectra \begin{equation} \xymatrix{ K(R, I) \ar[d] \ar[r] & K(S, J) \ar[d] \\ \mathbb{K}(R, I) \ar[r] & \mathbb{K}(S, J) }\end{equation} is cartesian.

nodes.name: Square of connective and nonconnective relative K-theory
nodes.statement: \xymatrix{ K(R, I) \ar[d] \ar[r] & K(S, J) \ar[d] \\ \mathbb{K}(R, I) \ar[r] & \mathbb{K}(S, J) }
nodes.label: Ksquare

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 4.34
nodes.statement_short: Compare fibers in degrees >= 0; Bass excision and K_0, K_1 control for henselian pairs.
nodes.statement: Let $F$ be the fiber of the top horizontal map and let $\mathbb{F}$ be the fiber of the bottom horizontal map. Note that the maps $K(R) \to \mathbb{K}(R), K(R/I) \to \mathbb{K}(R/I)$, etc.\ are equivalences in degrees $ \geq 0$; thus, taking fibers, the maps $K(R, I) \to \mathbb{K}(R, I)$ and $K(S, J) \to \mathbb{K}(S, J)$ are equivalences in degrees $\geq 0$. Taking fibers again, we find that the map $F \to \mathbb{F}$ is an equivalence in degrees $\geq 0$. On the other hand, $\mathbb{F}$ is concentrated in degrees $\geq 0$ (even $\geq 1$) by the excision theorem of Bass and Bass--Heller--Swan, \cite[Thm.~XII.8.3]{Bass}. Thus it suffices to show that $F$ is also concentrated in degrees $\geq 0$. But since $(R, I)$ and $(S, J)$ are henselian pairs, it follows by Lemma~\ref{K0invhenspair} that the maps $K_0(R) \to K_0(R/I), K_0(S) \to K_0(S/J)$ are isomorphisms and the maps $K_1(R) \to K_1(R/I), K_1(S) \to K_1(S/J)$ (which are the abelianizations of $GL_\infty(R) \to GL_\infty(R/I), GL_\infty(S) \to GL_\infty(S/J)$) are surjections; thus $K(R, I)$ and $K(S, J)$ are concentrated in degrees $\geq 1$, so that $F$ is concentrated in degrees $\geq 0$, as desired.

nodes.name: Excision for connective K^inv on henselian pairs
assumptions: Suppose $(R,I)$ is a henselian pair, and $f:R\rightarrow S$ is a ring homomorphism which restricts to an isomorphism from $I$ to an ideal $J\subset S$.
conclusions: the map $K^{\mathrm{inv}}(R, I) \to K^{\mathrm{inv}}(S, J)$ is an equivalence
nodes.statement: Suppose $(R,I)$ is a henselian pair, and $f:R\rightarrow S$ is a ring homomorphism which restricts to an isomorphism from $I$ to an ideal $J\subset S$. Then the map $K^{\mathrm{inv}}(R, I) \to K^{\mathrm{inv}}(S, J)$ is an equivalence.
nodes.label: replaceexcision

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary 4.35
nodes.statement_short: Combine the cartesian square with Theorem 4.33.
nodes.statement: Combining with the homotopy cartesian square \eqref{Ksquare} between relative connective and nonconnective $K$-theory, we find that the result now follows from Theorem~\ref{DKGHC}.

nodes.name: Rigidity of K^inv for henselian pairs (main theorem)
nodes.statement_short: For a henselian pair, relative K-theory and relative TC agree mod p via the cyclotomic trace.
assumptions: Let $(R, I)$ be a henselian pair.
conclusions: the map $K^{\mathrm{inv}}(R) \to K^{\mathrm{inv}}(R/I)$ becomes an equivalence modulo $p$
the map $K(R, I) \to \mathrm{TC}(R, I)$ becomes an equivalence modulo $p$
nodes.statement: Let $(R, I)$ be a henselian pair. Then for any prime number $p$, the map $K^{\mathrm{inv}}(R) \to K^{\mathrm{inv}}(R/I)$ becomes an equivalence modulo $p$. Equivalently, the map $K(R, I) \to \mathrm{TC}(R, I)$ becomes an equivalence modulo $p$.
nodes.label: mainthm

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 4.36
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to (Z semidirect I, I) by excision and verify the hypotheses of the axiomatic rigidity argument for K^inv/p. The base case uses Gabber rigidity away from p and Proposition 4.32 at p.
nodes.statement: By Corollary~\ref{replaceexcision}, it suffices to consider the case where $(R, I) = (\mathbb{Z} \ltimes I, I)$ where $I$ is a nonunital henselian ring. We now consider the functor \[ F: \mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}} \to \mathrm{Sp}, \quad F(I) = K^{\mathrm{inv}}(\mathbb{Z} \ltimes I, I)/p. \] By Propositions~\ref{Kpscoh} and \ref{TCpscoh}, $F$ is a projectively pseudocoherent functor. Implicit here is the statement (due to Quillen) that the $K$-groups of $\mathbb{Z}$ are finitely generated, as are the mod $p$ homotopy groups of $\mathrm{TC}(\mathbb{Z})$ (both of which follow from evaluating the projectively pseudocoherent functors $I \mapsto K(\mathbb{Z} \ltimes I), \mathrm{TC}(\mathbb{Z} \ltimes I)/p$ at $I = 0$). The assertion of the theorem is that $F=0$. We will show this by checking that $F$ satisfies the hypotheses of Proposition~\ref{pseudoargument}. First observe that $F$ sends a short exact sequence $I' \to I \twoheadrightarrow \overline{I}$ of nonunital henselian rings to a fiber sequence of spectra. To see this, we consider the diagram \[ \xymatrix{ F(I') \ar[d]^{\mathrm{id}} \ar[r] & F(I) \ar[d] \ar[r] & F(\overline{I}) \ar[d] \\ F(I') \ar[r] & K^{\mathrm{inv}}( \mathbb{Z} \ltimes I)/p \ar[r] & K^{\mathrm{inv}}( \mathbb{Z} \ltimes \overline{I})/p . }\] Note that the right-hand square is homotopy cartesian, so the top row is a fiber sequence if and only if the bottom row is a fiber sequence. But the bottom row is a fiber sequence by Corollary~\ref{replaceexcision} applied to the homomorphism $(\mathbb{Z}\ltimes I',I')\rightarrow (\mathbb{Z}\ltimes I, I')$. Next, we claim that if $I' \in \mathrm{Ring}^{\mathrm{nu,h}}$ is nilpotent, then $F(I') = 0$. This follows from Theorem~\ref{DGMthm} which shows that $K^{\mathrm{inv}}( \mathbb{Z} \ltimes I', I') = 0$. To complete the proof, i.e., to verify the conditions of Proposition~\ref{pseudoargument}, we need to check that \[ F( k\left\{x_1, \dots, x_n\right\}^+) = 0, \] whenever $k$ is a prime field. We write $k\left\{x_1, \dots, x_n\right\}$ for the henselization of the polynomial ring $k[x_1, \dots, x_n]$ at $(x_1, \dots, x_n)$, so $k\left\{x_1, \dots, x_n\right\}^+ \subset k\left\{x_1, \dots, x_n\right\}$ is the maximal ideal. Using Corollary~\ref{replaceexcision}, it suffices to show that the map $K^{\mathrm{inv}}(k\left\{x_1, \dots, x_n\right\}) \to K^{\mathrm{inv}}(k)$ is an equivalence modulo $p$. There are two cases for this. If $\mathrm{char}(k) \neq p$, this follows from Gabber rigidity. If $\mathrm{char}(k) = p$, this follows from Proposition~\ref{rigidity:henspaircharp}.

nodes.name: Relation to Gabber's proof of rigidity
nodes.statement: Recall that Gabber's proof \cite{gabber} of rigidity is cleanly separated into two halves: the first half reduces the general case to the case of henselizations of smooth algebras over a field at a rational point, and the second half proves that case. In our proof above, we only need to invoke the second half of Gabber's work, which is also covered by Gillet--Thomason \cite{GT}. However, our entire line of reasoning is in some sense modeled on the first half of Gabber's proof. (The exceptions are Proposition \ref{rigidity:henspaircharp}, which is the new characteristic $p$ ingredient, and the commutation of $\mathrm{TC}/p$ with filtered colimits, which is a necessary technical statement.) So we are not really avoiding the first half of Gabber's proof, just explicating it in a modified context. Let us note in particular that the projective pseudocoherence of $K$-theory is our replacement for Suslin's ``method of universal homotopies" from \cite{Suslinlocal}, which has been crucial to many of the known rigidity results in $K$-theory.

nodes.name: Easier proof for F_p-algebras
nodes.statement: While the the full strength of pseudocoherence appears to be necessary to obtain results for $\mathbb{Z}$-algebras, the result for henselian pairs of $\mathbb{F}_p$-algebras follows from Proposition~\ref{rigidity:henspaircharp} and the observation that $K, \mathrm{TC}/p$ commutes with filtered colimits of $\mathbb{F}_p$-algebras. One can then extend the result to $\mathbb{Z}_p$-algebras using the $p$-adic continuity statement of \cite{GHlocal} (and a similar filtered colimit argument). Thus, for $\mathbb{Z}_p$-algebras at least, one can prove the main result purely using the classical approach to $\mathrm{TC}$ and ingredients predating \cite{nikolaus-scholze}.
nodes.label: rem:fpcaseeasier

nodes.name: Rigidity fails integrally
nodes.statement_short: Counterexample: for the perfection of F_p[[x]], K_1 relative to its henselian ideal is not derived p-complete.
nodes.statement: Theorem~\ref{mainthm} is false integrally; that is, the integral Dundas--Goodwillie--McCarthy theorem does not hold for henselian pairs. As an example, let $(R, \mathfrak{m})$ be a henselian local $\mathbb{F}_p$-algebra with residue field $\mathbb{F}_p$. Then $\mathrm{TC}(R), \mathrm{TC}(\mathbb{F}_p)$ are $p$-complete spectra, so $\mathrm{TC}_1(R, \mathfrak{m})$ is a derived $p$-adically complete abelian group. However, $K_1(R, \mathfrak{m}) =\mathrm{ker}(R^{\times} \to \mathbb{F}_p^{\times})$ which will essentially never be derived $p$-complete. For instance, consider the power series ring $R_0 = \mathbb{F}_p[[x]]$ and let $R = (R_0)_{\mathrm{perf}}$ be the perfection of $R_0$. We have a surjection $R \to \mathbb{F}_p$, whose kernel is the henselian ideal $I = \bigcup (x^{1/p^n})$. In this case, $\mathrm{ker}(R^{\times} \to \mathbb{F}_p^{\times})$ is a nonzero $\mathbb{Z}[1/p]$-module, which in particular is not derived $p$-complete.

nodes.name: Continuity question in algebraic K-theory
nodes.statement_short: How close is K(R) -> lim K(R/I^s) to an equivalence?
nodes.statement: Let $R$ be a ring and $I$ be an ideal. How close is the map \begin{equation} K(R) \longrightarrow \varprojlim_s K(R/I^s) \end{equation} to being an equivalence?

nodes.name: Continuity map
nodes.statement: K(R) \longrightarrow \varprojlim_s K(R/I^s)
nodes.label: contmap

nodes.name: Continuity of K reduces to continuity of TC
assumptions: if $(R, I)$ is a henselian pair
nodes.statement:
In order to apply our earlier results to this question, we observe that if $(R, I)$ is a henselian pair  then Theorem~\ref{mainthm} implies that 
the map \eqref{contmap} becomes an equivalence modulo $p$ if and only if the
corresponding map $\mathrm{TC}(R) \to \varprojlim_s \mathrm{TC}(R/I^s)$ becomes an equivalence
modulo $p$.

nodes.name: F-finite F_p-algebra
nodes.statement: An $\mathbb{F}_p$-algebra $R$ is said to be \emph{$F$-finite} if the absolute Frobenius map $R \to R$ is finite, in other words if $R$ is a finitely generated module over its subring of $p^\sub{th}$-powers.
nodes.label: Ffinite

nodes.name: Mod p equivalence of THH from derived mod p equivalence
assumptions: Let $R \to R'$ be a map of commutative rings such that the map $R \otimes^{\mathbb{L}}_{\mathbb{Z}} \mathbb{F}_p \to R' \otimes^{\mathbb{L}}_{\mathbb{Z}} \mathbb{F}_p$ is an equivalence.
conclusions: $\mathrm{THH}(R) \to \mathrm{THH}(R')$ is a mod $p$ equivalence
nodes.statement: Let $R \to R'$ be a map of commutative rings such that the map $R \otimes^{\mathbb{L}}_{\mathbb{Z}} \mathbb{F}_p \to R' \otimes^{\mathbb{L}}_{\mathbb{Z}} \mathbb{F}_p$ is an equivalence. Then $\mathrm{THH}(R) \to \mathrm{THH}(R')$ is a mod $p$ equivalence.
nodes.label: modplemma0

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 5.2
nodes.statement_short: Tensor powers and colimits preserve mod p equivalences.
nodes.statement: The hypothesis is equivalent to saying that $HR\rightarrow HR'$ is a mod $p$ equivalence of spectra. It follows that $(HR)^{\otimes n}\rightarrow (HR')^{\otimes n}$ is a mod $p$ equivalence for all $n\geq 0$, and hence that $\mathrm{THH}(R)\rightarrow \mathrm{THH}(R')$ is a mod $p$ equivalence, since mod $p$ equivalences are preserved under colimits.

nodes.name: THH of a noetherian ring and its p-completion agree mod p
assumptions: Let $R$ be a noetherian ring and let $\widehat{R}_p$ be its $p$-adic completion
conclusions: the map $\mathrm{THH}(R) \to \mathrm{THH}(\widehat{R}_p)$ is a mod $p$ equivalence
nodes.statement: Let $R$ be a noetherian ring and let $\widehat{R}_p$ be its $p$-adic completion (which is also the derived $p$-adic completion, as $R$ has bounded $p$-power torsion). Then the map $\mathrm{THH}(R) \to \mathrm{THH}(\widehat{R}_p)$ is a mod $p$ equivalence.
nodes.label: modplemma

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 5.3
nodes.statement_short: Bounded p-torsion gives a derived mod p equivalence; apply Lemma 5.2.
nodes.statement: A noetherian ring has bounded $p$-torsion, which implies that the map $R \to \widehat{R}_p$ induces an equivalence $R \otimes^{\mathbb L}_\mathbb Z \mathbb{F}_p \simeq \widehat{R}_p \otimes^{\mathbb L}_\mathbb Z \mathbb{F}_p$. Thus the statement follows from Lemma \ref{modplemma0}.

nodes.name: Continuity of THH for F-finite complete noetherian rings
assumptions: Let $R$ be a noetherian ring which is complete along an ideal $I\subseteq R$, and suppose that $R/pR$ is $F$-finite.
conclusions: the map $\mathrm{THH}(R) \to \varprojlim_s \mathrm{THH}(R/I^s)$ is an equivalence modulo $p$
nodes.statement: Let $R$ be a noetherian ring which is complete along an ideal $I\subseteq R$, and suppose that $R/pR$ is $F$-finite. Then the map $\mathrm{THH}(R) \to \varprojlim_s \mathrm{THH}(R/I^s)$ is an equivalence modulo $p$.
nodes.label: THHcont

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 5.4
nodes.statement_short: Pass to the p-completion and apply Dundas--Morrow continuity, then Lemma 5.3.
nodes.statement: First we note that $\widehat R_p = \varprojlim_s \widehat{R/I^s}_p$ and $\widehat{R/I^s}_p = \widehat R_p /I^s\widehat R_p$. Indeed, $R$ being noetherian, we have that on finitely generated $R$-modules the $p$-adic completion identifies with the derived $p$-completion. It therefore preserves short exact sequences and sequential inverse limits along surjective transition maps, as these are examples of derived limits. In particular, $\widehat R_p$ is $I\widehat R_p$-adically complete. Therefore, the canonical map \[ \mathrm{THH}(\widehat{R}_p)/p \longrightarrow \varprojlim_s \mathrm{THH}( \widehat{R}_p/I^s \widehat{R}_p)/p\] is an equivalence by \cite[Thm.~4.5]{DundasMorrow}. But by the above, each quotient $\widehat R_p/I^s\widehat R_p$ coincides with the $p$-adic completion of $R/I^s$, so that applying Lemma~\ref{modplemma} to $R$ and to each $R/I^s $ completes the proof.

nodes.name: Continuity criterion for K-theory
nodes.statement_short: For complete noetherian rings with F-finite reduction mod p, K/p is continuous.
assumptions: Let $R$ be a noetherian ring which is complete along an ideal $I$, and suppose that $R/pR$ is $F$-finite.
conclusions: the map $K(R) \to \varprojlim_s K(R/I^s)$ is an equivalence modulo $p$
nodes.statement: Let $R$ be a noetherian ring which is complete along an ideal $I$, and suppose that $R/pR$ is $F$-finite. Then the map $K(R) \to \varprojlim_s K(R/I^s)$ is an equivalence modulo $p$.
nodes.label: Kcont

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 5.5
nodes.statement_short: Main theorem reduces to TC, then to THH by Remark 2.8, then Proposition 5.4.
nodes.statement: Using Theorem~\ref{mainthm}, the result reduces to the statement that $\mathrm{TC}(R)/p \to \varprojlim_s \mathrm{TC}(R/I^s)/p$ is an equivalence. By Remark~\ref{TCinvlim}, this in turn follows from the analogous statement for $\mathrm{THH}$, which is given by Proposition~\ref{THHcont}.

nodes.name: Continuity is equivalent to rigidity
nodes.statement_short: Via Neron--Popescu desingularization and Elkik, Theorem 5.5 implies Theorem 4.36.
nodes.statement: One can see that Theorem~\ref{Kcont} is in fact equivalent to Theorem~\ref{mainthm} (our main theorem on henselian pairs). Indeed, suppose Theorem~\ref{Kcont} is known, and let $(R,I)$ be a henselian pair. We want to show that $K^{\mathrm{inv}}(R)/p\rightarrow K^{\mathrm{inv}}(R/I)/p$ is an equivalence. Since $K$ and $\mathrm{TC}/p$ commute with filtered colimits, so does $K^{\mathrm{inv}}/p$, hence we can assume $(R,I)$ is the henselization of a finite type $\mathbb{Z}$-algebra at an ideal. Let $\widehat{R}$ denote the $I$-adic completion of $R$. By N\'eron--Popescu desingularization \cite{Popescu1, Popescu2} (see also \cite[Tag 07BW]{stacks-project}), applicable in view of the geometric regularity of $R \to \widehat{R}$ (see \cite[7.8.3(v)]{EGA_IV_2}), the map $R\rightarrow \widehat{R}$ is ind-smooth, i.e., we can write $\widehat{R}$ as a filtered colimit of smooth $R$-algebras. Given a smooth $R$-algebra $A$ and a map $A \to \widehat{R}$ of $R$-algebras, it follows that the map $R \to A$ admits a section by Elkik's theorem (Theorem~\ref{elkikthm}). Therefore, we deduce that $R\rightarrow \widehat{R}$ is a filtered colimit of split injections. Thus the claim for $(R,I)$ (i.e., that $K^{\mathrm{inv}}(R)/p \to K^{\mathrm{inv}}(R/I)/p$ is an equivalence) will follow from the claim for $(\widehat{R}, I \widehat{R})$. (This is a standard Artin approximation argument.) However, by the above continuity in $K$ and $\mathrm{TC}$, we have $$K^{\mathrm{inv}}(\widehat{R})/p\overset{\simeq}{\rightarrow}\varprojlim K^{\mathrm{inv}}(R/I^n)/p.$$ On the other hand, the right hand side is a constant limit with value $K^{\mathrm{inv}}(R/I)/p$, by Theorem~\ref{DGMthm}. This gives the claim for $(\widehat{R}, I\widehat{R})$, and therefore in general, by the above argument.
nodes.label: henspairequivtocontinuity

nodes.name: Discontinuity of K-theory for non-F-finite fields
nodes.statement_short: For a non-F-finite field k, K(k[[t]])/p -> lim K(k[t]/t^s)/p is not surjective on pi_2.
assumptions: Let $k$ be an field of characteristic $p$ which is not $F$-finite, i.e., any $p$-basis
conclusions: the map $K(k[[t]])/p \to \varprojlim_s K(k[t]/(t^s))/p$ is not an equivalence
the map on $\pi_2$ is not surjective
nodes.statement: Let $k$ be an field of characteristic $p$ which is not $F$-finite, i.e., any $p$-basis\footnote{We refer to \cite[\S26]{Matsumura1989} for a reminder on the notion of a $p$-basis, including the fact that a collection of elements $\{b_i\}$ of $k$ forms part of a $p$-basis if and only if their differentials $\{db_i\}$ are linearly independent in $\Omega^1_k$.} of $k$ has infinite cardinality. Then the map $K(k[[t]])/p \to \varprojlim_s K(k[t]/(t^s))/p$ is not an equivalence; more precisely, the map on $\pi_2$ is not surjective.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 5.7
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to Milnor K_2 and detect symbols with dlog; following Bloch--Esnault--Kerz, build a compatible system of symbols whose weights grow too fast to lift.
nodes.statement: We begin with several straightforward reductions to Milnor $K$-theory. Firstly, since $k[[t]]^\times$ is $p$-torsion-free, the canonical map $K_2(k[[t]])/p\to \pi_2 (K(k[[t]])/p)$ is an isomorphism. The $p$-torsion in the pro abelian group $\{k[t]/(t^s)^\times\}_s$ is also zero, since the transition map $k[t]/(t^{ps})^\times\to k[t]/(t^s)^\times$ clearly kills all $p$-torsion in the domain, and therefore $\{K_2(k[t]/(t^s))/p\}_s\to \{\pi_2(K(k[t]/(t^s))/p) \}_s$ is an isomorphism of pro abelian groups. Secondly, $k[[t]]$ and $k[t]/(t^s)$ are local rings with infinite residue field, whence a classical result in algebraic $K$-theory \cite[\S8]{vanderKallen1977} states that $K_2^M(k[[t]])\stackrel{\simeq}{\to} K_2(k[[t]])$ and $K_2^M(k[t]/(t^s))\stackrel{\simeq}{\to} K_2(k[t]/(t^s))$. Finally, the canonical map $\pi_2 (\varprojlim_s K(k[t]/(t^s))/p)\to \varprojlim_s\pi_2( K(k[t]/(t^s))/p)$ is surjective, by the Milnor sequence. In conclusion, to prove the theorem it is sufficient to show that the canonical map $K_2^M(k[[t]])/p\to\varprojlim_sK_2^M(k[t]/(t^s))/p$ is not surjective. To do this, we will detect symbols using the $\mathrm{dlog}$ maps from $K_2^M$ to absolute K\"ahler differentials $\Omega^2_{-}:=\Omega^2_{-/\mathbb F_p}$: \[\xymatrix{ \Omega^2_{k[[t]]}\ar[r]&\varprojlim_s\Omega^2_{k[t]/(t^s)}\\ K_2^M(k[[t]])/p\ar[u]_{\operatorname{dlog}}\ar[r] &\varprojlim_s K_2^M(k[t]/(t^s))/p\ar[u]_{\operatorname{dlog}} }\] It remains to construct an element in the bottom right of the diagram whose image in the top right does not come from the top left. We now closely follow Bloch--Esnault--Kerz, with the necessary modifications to deal with the fact that we will eventually need to restrict to dlog forms. Given any map of rings $R\to S$ and differential form $\tau\in\Omega^2_{S/R}$, define its {\em weight} $w(\tau)$ to be the smallest integer $n$ for which it is possible to write $\tau=\sum_{i=1}^na_idb_i\wedge dc_i$ for some $a_i,b_i,c_i\in S$. If $\ell$ is a subfield of $k$ and $b_1,\dots,b_n,c_1,\dots,c_n\in k$ form part of a $p$-basis for $k$ relative to $\ell$, then the elements $d b_1,\dots,d b_n,d c_1,\dots,d c_n$ are linearly independent in the $k$-vector space $\Omega^1_{k/\ell}$ and so this element $\sum_{i=1}^ndb_i\wedge dc_i$ has weight $\ge n$ in $\Omega^2_{k/\ell}$ (Lemma~\ref{linalg} below). Next consider the derivation $$k[t]/(t^s) \rightarrow \Omega^1_k \otimes_k k[t]/(t^s)$$ which ``holds $t$ constant", so $\sum_n c_n t^n \mapsto \sum_n (dc_n)t^n$. This extends by multiplicativity to a map $$\Omega^\ast_{k[t]/(t^s)}\rightarrow \Omega^\ast_k \otimes_k k[t]/(t^s)$$ which splits the canonical map $\Omega^\ast_k\otimes_k k[t]/(t^s)\rightarrow \Omega^\ast_{k[t]/(t^s)}$. Restricting to degree $\ast=2$ and passing to the limit as $s\to\infty$ defines \[e:\varprojlim_s\Omega^2_{k[t]/(t^s)}\longrightarrow \varprojlim_s\Omega^2_k\otimes_kk[t]/(t^s),\] where each element on the right may be expressed as $\sum_{j\ge 0}\tau_i t^i$ for some unique $\tau_0,\tau_1,\dots\in \Omega^2_k$ (the {\em $t$-adic coefficients} of the element). Bloch--Esnault--Kerz \cite[Lem.~B2]{BlochEsnaultKerz2013} show (assuming $k = \mathbb{C}$, but the argument works in general) that the image of the composition \[\Omega^2_{k[[t]]}\longrightarrow \varprojlim_s\Omega^2_{k[t]/(t^s)}\longrightarrow \varprojlim_s\Omega^2_k\otimes_kk[t]/(t^s)\] lands inside the set of those elements $\sum_{j\ge 0}\tau_j t^j$ whose $t$-adic coefficients satisfy the following: there exists $N\ge0$ such that $w(\tau_j)\le N\binom{j+2}j$ for all $j\ge0$. We are now prepared to complete the proof by constructing a bad element of $\varprojlim_s K_2^M(k[t]/(t^s))/p$. First pick a sequence $0<w_1<w_2<\cdots$ of integers growing sufficiently fast such that no value of $N$ satisfies $w_j\le N\binom{2j}{2j-2}$ for all $j\ge1$. Then pick a sequence of subfields $\mathbb F_p=k_0\subset k_1\subset k_2\subset\cdots$ of $k$ such that any $p$-basis for $k_j$ relative to $k_{j-1}$ has $\ge2w_j$ elements; let $b_1^{(j)},\cdots,b_{w_j}^{(j)},c_1^{(j)},\cdots,c_{w_j}^{(j)}\in k_i$ be part of such a relative $p$-basis. Set \[f_s:=\sum_{j=1}^{s-1}\sum_{i=1}^{w_j}\{1+t^jb_i^{(j)},1+t^jc_i^{(j)}\}\in K_2^M(k[t]/(t^{s}))/p\] and note that the transition map $K_2^M(k[t]/(t^{s}))/p\to K_2^M(k[t]/(t^{s-1}))/p$ exactly kills the $j=s-1$ part of the sum and therefore sends $f_s$ to $f_{s-1}$; we therefore may define $f:=\varprojlim_s f_s\in\varprojlim_sK_2^M(k[t]/(t^{s}))/p$. Let $\sum_{i\ge 1}\tau_it^i$ be the expansion of $e(\mathrm{dlog} f)\in\varprojlim_s\Omega^2_k\otimes_kk[t]/(t^s)$. Noting that \[\mathrm{dlog}(1+t^jb)\wedge\mathrm{dlog}(1+t^jc)\equiv t^{2j}da\wedge db\text{ mod }dt,\,t^{3j}\] with all the higher order terms given by various expressions in $b,c$, we see that \[\tau_{2s-2}\equiv\sum_{i=1}^{w_{s}}b_i^{(s)}\wedge c_i^{(s)} \text{ mod }{\Omega^2_{k_{s-1}}}.\] By the second paragraph of the proof we deduce that the image of $\tau_{2s-2}$ in $\Omega^2_{k/k_{s-1}}$ has weight $\ge w_s$, whence a fortiori $w(\tau_{2s-2})\ge w_s$. By choice of the sequence $0< w_1<\cdots$, it follows that $\mathrm{dlog} f$ cannot be lifted to $\Omega^2_{k[[t]]}$, which completes the proof.

nodes.name: Weight of a 2-form
nodes.statement:
Given a 2-form $\omega \in \bigwedge^2 V$, we define the \emph{weight}
of $\omega$ to be the minimal $n$ such that there exist elements
$\left\{x_i, y_i|1 \leq i \leq n\right\} \subset V$ such that
$\omega = \sum_{i=1}^n x_i \wedge y_i$.

nodes.name: Weight of a sum of independent wedges
assumptions: Let $\left\{u_1, \dots, u_n, v_1, \dots, v_n\right\}$ be linearly independent in $V$.
conclusions: the form $\sum_{i=1}^n u_i \wedge v_i$ has weight $n$
nodes.statement: Let $\left\{u_1, \dots, u_n, v_1, \dots, v_n\right\}$ be linearly independent in $V$. Then the form $\sum_{i=1}^n u_i \wedge v_i$ has weight $n$.
nodes.label: linalg

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 5.8
nodes.statement_short: Rank of the interior product map bounds weight.
nodes.statement: Recall that we have an \emph{interior product} $V^{\vee} \otimes \bigwedge^2 V \to V$ given by $v \otimes (x \wedge y) \mapsto \left \langle v, x\right\rangle y - \left \langle v, y\right\rangle x$. Given $\omega \in \bigwedge^2 V$, we obtain a map $f_\omega: V^{\vee} \to V$. If $\omega$ has weight $w$, then the rank of $f_{\omega}$ is at most $2w$. Completing $\left\{u_1,\dots, u_n, v_1, \dots, v_n\right\}$ to a basis of $V$ and forming the dual basis, one now sees that the rank of $f_{\omega_0}$ for $\omega_0 = \sum_{i=1}^n u_i \wedge v_i$ is $2n$; together, this implies the lemma.

nodes.name: p-adic continuity of K-theory
nodes.statement: Let $R$ be a commutative ring. We say that $K$-theory is \emph{$p$-adically continuous} for $R$ if the map of spectra $K(R) \to \varprojlim_i K(R/p^iR)$ is an equivalence modulo $p$.

nodes.name: Geisser--Hesselholt p-adic continuity
assumptions: If $R$ is a local ring which is $p$-torsion-free and henselian along $(p)$
conclusions: $K$-theory is $p$-adically continuous at $R$
nodes.statement: If $R$ is a local ring which is $p$-torsion-free and henselian along $(p)$, then $K$-theory is $p$-adically continuous at $R$. Moreover, the map $K(R)/p \to \left\{ K(R/p^iR)/p\right\}_{i \geq 1}$ induces an isomorphism of pro abelian groups upon applying $\pi_j$ for any $j$.
nodes.label: GHcontinuity

nodes.name: K^inv for E_1-ring spectra
nodes.statement: The functors $K, \mathrm{TC}$ are defined not only for ordinary rings $R$, but more generally for arbitrary $\mathbb{E}_1$-ring spectra $R$. For such $R$, we define $K^{\mathrm{inv}}(R)$ similarly, as the fiber of the cyclotomic trace $K(R) \to \mathrm{TC}(R)$.

nodes.name: Dundas--Goodwillie--McCarthy for connective E_1-rings
assumptions:
if $R$
is a connective $\mathbb{E}_1$-algebra
conclusions:
the map $K^{\mathrm{inv}}(R) \to K^{\mathrm{inv}}(\pi_0 R)$
is an equivalence
nodes.statement:
Part of the theorem of Dundas--Goodwillie--McCarthy \cite{dgm} states that if $R$
is a connective $\mathbb{E}_1$-algebra, then the map $K^{\mathrm{inv}}(R) \to K^{\mathrm{inv}}(\pi_0 R)$
is an equivalence.

nodes.name: Nilpotent and quickly converging towers of abelian groups
nodes.statement: Let $\left\{A_i\right\}_{i \geq 1}$ be a tower of abelian groups. We say that the tower is \emph{nilpotent} if there exists $N> 0$ such that all the maps $A_{i+N} \to A_i$ are zero. We say that the tower is \emph{quickly converging} if there exists $r \in \mathbb{Z}_{>0}$ such that the tower $\{\mathrm{im}(A_{i+r} \to A_i)\}_{i\ge1}$ is eventually constant. This is stronger than the Mittag--Leffler condition.
nodes.label: quickconvab

nodes.name: Quickly converging towers form an abelian subcategory
nodes.statement:
By \cite[Lemma 3.10]{Mthick}, it follows that the collection of towers of
abelian groups which are quickly converging forms an abelian subcategory of the
category of towers which is closed under extensions.

nodes.name: Quickly converging towers differ from their limit by nilpotent towers
assumptions:
if $\left\{A_i\right\}$ is a quickly converging tower and
$A$ is the inverse limit
nodes.statement:
It thus follows that if $\left\{A_i\right\}$ is a quickly converging tower and
$A$ is the inverse limit, then the kernel and cokernel of the map of towers
$\left\{A\right\} \to \left\{A_i\right\}$ are both nilpotent.

nodes.name: Quickly converging towers are generated by nilpotent and constant towers
nodes.statement:
In particular, the category of quickly converging towers is the smallest abelian 
subcategory containing the nilpotent towers and the constant towers which is
closed under extensions.

nodes.name: Nilpotent and quickly converging towers of spectra
nodes.statement: Let $\left\{X_i\right\}_{i \geq 1}$ be a tower in $\mathrm{Sp}$, i.e., $\{X_i\}_{i\ge1}\in\operatorname{Tow}(\mathrm{Sp}):=\operatorname{Fun}(\mathbb N^\sub{op},\mathrm{Sp})$. We say that the tower is \emph{nilpotent} if there exists $N> 0$ such that all the maps $X_{i+N} \to X_i$ are nullhomotopic. The collection of nilpotent towers forms a thick subcategory of the stable $\infty$-category $\operatorname{Tow}(\mathrm{Sp})$. We say that a tower $\left\{X_i\right\}$ is \emph{quickly converging} if the cofiber of the map of towers $\left\{X\right\} \to \left\{X_i\right\}$ is nilpotent, where $X:=\varprojlim_iX_i$, or equivalently if $\left\{X_i\right\}$ lies in the smallest thick subcategory of towers containing the constant towers and the nilpotent towers.

nodes.name: Quick convergence and homotopy groups
assumptions: Let $\left\{X_i\right\}_{i\ge1}$ be a tower in $\mathrm{Sp}$.
conclusions: the tower $\left\{\pi_j X_i\right\}$ of abelian groups is quickly converging for each $j$
nodes.statement: Let $\left\{X_i\right\}_{i\ge1}$ be a tower in $\mathrm{Sp}$. If $\left\{X_i\right\}$ is quickly converging, the tower $\left\{\pi_j X_i\right\}$ of abelian groups is quickly converging for each $j$. The converse holds if we suppose that each $X_i$ has homotopy groups concentrated in the fixed range $[a,b]$.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 5.13
nodes.statement_short: Cite Mathew's lemma for one direction; devissage to a single degree for the converse.
nodes.statement: It follows from \cite[Lemma 3.11]{Mthick} that if $\left\{X_i\right\}$ is quickly converging, then the towers of homotopy groups are quickly converging. Indeed, if $\left\{X_i\right\}$ is nilpotent or constant, then the tower of homotopy groups is clearly quickly converging, and the referenced result shows that the condition on homotopy groups is stable in cofiber sequences of towers. For the converse direction, a d\'evissage reduces to the case where $a= b$. In this case, it follows from the paragraph following Definition~\ref{quickconvab}: that is, quickly convergent towers of abelian groups are built up from constant and nilpotent towers.

nodes.name: Almost nilpotent and almost quickly converging towers
